isw.title: Every basin models ISW numerically, but not every model estimates depletion
isw.body: All six subbasins characterize interconnected surface water with a numerical groundwater–surface water model, the approach the literature calls the gold standard. The models report slightly different outputs however. Merced and Salinas Valley isolate pumping-attributable depletion by running the model with and without pumping. Kaweah's model is not yet calibrated for streams, so it substitutes an analytical depletion function. East Turlock, Colusa and Yolo report net stream–aquifer exchange from all causes and label it depletion. While Colusa and Yolo describe their ISW results as provisional or uncalibrated on most streams.

isw.title: Groundwater levels stand in for modeled depletion
isw.body: No basin uses model output as its ISW compliance measure. Five test compliance on groundwater elevations at near-stream wells, and Salinas Valley, Colusa and Yolo cite EDF (2018) for that proxy. The plans give their reasons for using groundwater levels as proxies. They mention that models are not calibrated to individual streams, uncertainty is too large to quantify depletion reliably, and, in Salinas Valley, the judgment that annual model updates are unrealistic. Merced defends the proxy, revealing that it ran a scenario at its thresholds, which added 38,000 AFY of depletion (about 1.6% of surface outflow). The GSP judged the depletion small enough for groundwater levels to protect streams.

isw.title: Thresholds and undesirable results are defined on groundwater levels
isw.body: Five of the six basins set ISW criteria on groundwater elevations. Merced does so by carrying over its chronic-lowering thresholds rather than setting ISW-specific ones. What GSAs count as an undesirable result varies widely: any one shallow well in Salinas Valley, half of a river's wells for two consecutive falls in East Turlock, the same three of twelve wells for 24 months in Colusa, and more than half the wells in two or more management zones in Yolo. Kaweah has not defined a basin-wide undesirable result. Its self-described "placeholder" criteria set one flow threshold, on one reach of the Lower Kaweah River.

isw.title: Depletion volumes are not tied to thresholds, or always to pumping
isw.body: Published depletion volumes have not yet been used to set or test a threshold. They are used as descriptive metrics only. Merced estimates 504,400 AFY of pumping-attributable depletion and uses none of it in its criteria. Salinas Valley's 2020 volumetric threshold of 69,700 AF/yr was net exchange from all causes. Later, a no-pumping run put pumping's share at 8,400 AF/yr, and Amendment 1 replaced the volume with a groundwater-level proxy. East Turlock's annual "depletion" totals include a 28,700 AF net gain on the San Joaquin. They do not come from a with-and-without-pumping comparison, so none is attributed to pumping.

isw.title: Monitoring networks differ in size and depth, and typically grow from grants
isw.body: The wells behind the groundwater-level proxy vary widely. Salinas Valley's ISW network ran on one usable well for its entire evaluation period, after a second proved to be screened beneath the aquitard. Colusa uses 12 near-stream wells under 200 feet deep and Yolo 17 shallow wells across five zones, while East Turlock's shallow network includes wells screened hundreds of feet below the water table. New ISW wells and gages are mostly grant-funded, and Colusa and Yolo list remedies without dates or funding.

isw.title: "Significant and unreasonable" designations are mostly anchored to the last drought
isw.body: SGMA leaves the definition of significant and unreasonable depletion to each GSA, and most use a recent drought to make those definitions. Fall 2015 groundwater levels are used in East Turlock and Colusa (plus 10 feet of "operational flexibility" in Colusa), and 2015 levels plus one foot in Salinas Valley. Kaweah is the exception, anchoring to streamflow rather than groundwater. It uses low flows below WY 2022 levels on one reach. Yolo sets its Upper Sacramento thresholds 63–65 feet below its objectives to allow for expected cuts in surface-water deliveries. The literature identifies a potential ecological alternative: flow criteria set from habitat needs, as in the California Environmental Flows Framework.

isw.title: Uncertainty in depletion estimates is rarely quantified
isw.body: The literature calls out the importance of reporting uncertainty alongside a depletion estimate. Kaweah is the one basin to do so numerically. The reported 1.4 cfs estimate for the Lower Kaweah carries a 90% likelihood range from 100,000 Monte Carlo runs, along with published model calibration statistics. Colusa labels its ISW conclusions provisional and the other basins describe uncertainty in prose, but none bound a depletion volume. Merced's 2026 Rules add a numeric uncertainty buffer, but to the groundwater-level trigger, not to depletion.

mlrp.title: Repurposing happens through several programs, each reporting to a different agency
mlrp.body: Four subbasins hold Department of Conservation MLRP block grants of $8.89–10 million, but the grantee varies. The grantee is held by a GSA in Merced, the subbasin in East Turlock and Kaweah, and a regional non-GSA water management group in Salinas Valley. Other repurposing programs operate alongside them. Merced's fee-funded Phase 1 Land Repurposing Program had repurposed 14,128 acres by WY 2025. East Turlock runs a three-year Incentivized Fallowing Program. Kaweah also took part in DWR's LandFlex, which idled land near at-risk domestic wells.

mlrp.title: Repurposing goals are set in acre-feet, in acres, or not at all
mlrp.body: Merced commits to 25,911 AF of savings over five years and measured about 4,655 AF in WY 2025. That is roughly 10% short on an annual basis. East Turlock targets 21,000 acres, 3,880 more than its own suitability analysis could locate with the difference designated as a "Miscellaneous Repurposing" placeholder carrying 19% of the headline water benefit. Kaweah's MLRP targets are acres only, targeting about 238 acres of recharge basins and 65 or more of habitat, with no water figure identified. Salinas Valley's repurposing action names a benefit type with no quantity found in the reviewed text.

mlrp.title: Water savings are calculated after implementation, before it, or not at all
mlrp.body: Merced measures savings after implementation, parcel by parcel, with OpenET through its accounting platform. It found reductions lower than expected because orchard trees and wet-year soil moisture kept transpiring. East Turlock estimates savings once, beforehand (2.7 AF per acre from satellite ET, revised to 2.9 with its groundwater model three months later), and exempts enrolled parcels from ET measurement. For Kaweah, a fallowed field simply stops being debited, and its three GSAs each treat fallow land differently.

mlrp.title: Benefits beyond water are named and scored, but rarely measured
mlrp.body: Every grantee basin names ecological, community and economic benefits, and none measures a delivered outcome for them inside its repurposing program. Merced scores benefits at application on a points rubric with no published formula. East Turlock prices them. Rewilding pays $410 per acre per year more than extended fallowing for an identical water obligation, which makes that difference the price of habitat. Salinas Valley holds the most rigorous ecological method in the study, an annually repeatable vegetation threshold for groundwater-dependent ecosystems, but it is unadopted and measures groundwater depth rather than repurposing.

mlrp.title: Each basin decides differently where a repurposed parcel's allocation goes
mlrp.body: In Merced, enrolled landowners choose whether to give up their allocation. Most keep it, and the allocation can accumulate and be carried over or transferred. East Turlock rescinds the allocation of paid parcels for the agreement term, so a landowner cannot both be paid not to pump and keep the right to pump. Kaweah leaves the allocation portable, even between GSAs, but scales a transfer leave-behind by distance and has run pilot market auctions. Salinas Valley has no allocation system yet. It buys or leases the land, removing the pumper instead of regulating them.

mlrp.title: Parcels are chosen top-down by suitability analysis or bottom-up by landowner interest
mlrp.body: East Turlock sited its program with a suitability analysis. It used named stream buffers and slope thresholds layered over public datasets, ground-truthed with aerial imagery. Salinas Valley is building a recharge-suitability and multi-criteria decision tool with UC Davis. MKGSA uses Sustainable Conservation's Groundwater Recharge Assessment Tool to pursue parcels for acquisition, though its plan declares the tool advisory. Merced instead relies on landowner applications, scored on a rubric whose formula and award threshold are unpublished. In Colusa and Yolo, repurposing-type projects are proposed and run mostly by partners such as The Nature Conservancy, districts and community groups.

community.title: Every basin tests groundwater thresholds against well depths, but methods differ
community.body: All six basins compare well depths with groundwater thresholds. Colusa estimates 99 affected domestic wells at its revised minimum thresholds, down from 589. Kaweah estimates about 350 could be affected. Turlock found 208 of 7,767 supply wells, of all types, likely dry at its thresholds. Merced checks domestic and public supply well depths, Salinas Valley used only 14 accurately located wells for its threshold check, and Yolo compares well screens by township area. The analyses checked do not report results separately for disadvantaged communities.

community.title: Domestic well records have gaps in location and construction
community.body: Gaps in well records limit these analyses. In Colusa, about half of the state well completion records lack screen depth, and many locations are approximate. Turlock mostly compares water levels with total well depth because screen intervals are rarely recorded. Salinas Valley reports that most state records are mapped to the center of a land survey section. Mid-Kaweah says the exact locations of most domestic wells are not well understood. Merced's analysis did not have pump setting information.

community.title: GSAs are filling well data gaps in different ways
community.body: The Merced Irrigation-Urban GSA hired Self-Help Enterprises to contact landowners, which improved about 30 well records. Machine learning on well completion reports improved location data for about 400. In Salinas Valley, a 2024 county water agency ordinance extended well registration to all wells. Kaweah's GSAs committed to phased, voluntary registration. Yolo is improving its records with a federal grant and an AI-assisted method. Colusa lists inventory and registration as potential studies, and Turlock lists registration as a possible program.

community.title: Basins differ in what they identify as a community benefit
community.body: Merced's repurposing application awards points for drinking water security, workforce, green space, recreation, air quality and education benefits. Turlock's GSP says repurposing benefits for disadvantaged communities overlap with sustainability benefits, and adds recreation and public health. Salinas Valley's 2025 evaluation was asking communities to identify desired benefits. East Kaweah describes drinking water, habitat and walking trail benefits for a project near Seville. Colusa names domestic water supply as a recharge program objective. Yolo's project table has a yes-or-no disadvantaged community column, without a definition found.

community.title: Spanish-language access appears in most basins, in different forms
community.body: Turlock's GSP records a Spanish video, fact sheet, bill insert and surveys. It also notes a Spanish flyer for an EDF-partnered Water Leadership Institute and interpreters for technical advisory meetings on advance request. Merced offered Spanish translation at public workshops. Salinas Valley reports website translation, materials in two languages and interpretation at 2024 workshops. Colusa made meeting flyers in English and Spanish. Mid-Kaweah plans bilingual web materials and a translated workshop. Yolo's reviewed documents do not describe agency translation. Extending access to routine meetings and newer materials is an idea to explore.

community.title: GSAs reach growers and communities through varied products and programs
community.body: Kaweah's seasonal groundwater quality report points residents to free well testing and invites well registration. Salinas Valley added a story map. Castroville's water district identified a need for better outreach on how seawater intrusion could affect health, water bills and home values. East Turlock held workshops, office hours and a help line, and East Kaweah offers growers help with its water dashboard. Turlock held a Water Leadership Institute in 2021, and Salinas Valley planned one for early 2026, both with EDF as a partner. The documents searched do not direct residents to the Drinking Water Tool or CalEnviroScreen.
